items.text: Population JK-EGW objective (Eq. 1). M modalities with marginals mu^i on X^i, shared latent Z subset R^{d_z} with user-chosen marginal nu. S_eps({mu^i}, nu) = inf over couplings pi^i in Gamma(mu^i, nu) of sum_{i,j=1}^M int int K(x,x') ||z - z'||^2 dpi^i(x,z) dpi^j(x',z') + eps * sum_i KL(pi^i || mu^i (x) nu). The ordered double sum covers within-modality (i=j) and cross-modality (i != j) pairs. K: X x X -> R_{>=0} is a global affinity kernel on the disjoint union X of all modality spaces; eps > 0.
items.quote: For coupled samples (x, z) and (x′ , z ′ ), we assign the pairwise latent penalty K(x, x′ )∥z − z ′ ∥2 .

items.text: KL divergence used as the entropic regulariser: D_KL(alpha || beta) = int log(dalpha/dbeta) dalpha. In the discrete problem with uniform marginals mu_hat^i (x) nu_hat_n = (1/n^2) on each cell, KL(pi || mu (x) nu) = sum_{k,l} pi_kl log(n^2 pi_kl).
items.quote: Here, ϵ > 0 is the entropic regularization parameter, and DKL denotes the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence

items.text: K is assumed symmetric PSD with Mercer decomposition w.r.t. the mixture rho = (1/M) sum_i mu^i: K(x,x') = sum_r lambda_r phi'_r(x) phi'_r(x'). Scaled eigenfunctions phi_r = sqrt(lambda_r) phi'_r; Phi_R(x) = (phi_1(x),...,phi_R(x)); rank-R kernel K_R(x,x') = Phi_R(x)^T Phi_R(x'). Assumption 1: K(x,x) <= kappa^2; residual E_R = K - K_R; eta_R = sup_x sum_{r>R} phi_r(x)^2 -> 0.
items.quote: we assume that K is symmetric positive semidefinite, and thus admits a Mercer decomposition (Mercer, 1909) with respect to ρ

items.text: Rank-R JK-EGW objective (Eq. 2): S_eps^R is Eq. 1 with K(x,x') replaced by Phi_R(x)^T Phi_R(x'). Proposition 3: |S_eps - S_eps^R| <~ M^2 sigma eta_R when nu is 4-sub-Weibull with parameter sigma^2.
items.quote: We can thus introduce a rank-R JK-EGW objective by replacing K by its rank-R approximation,

items.text: Theorem 4 (population lifting). With m_Phi = sum_j int Phi_R dmu^j in R^R and modality cost c^i_{A,m}(x,z) = 2 Phi_R(x)^T m_Phi ||z||^2 - 4 <A, Phi_R(x) z^T>_F for A in R^{R x d_z}, S_eps^R = inf_A { 2||A||_F^2 + sum_i OT^i_{A,m,eps}(mu^i, nu) }, where OT^i is the linear EOT problem inf_{pi^i} int c^i dpi^i + eps KL(pi^i || mu^i (x) nu). The infimum is attained at some A* with ||A*||_F <= M kappa (2 sigma^2)^{1/4}.
items.quote: The lifted formulation introduces an auxiliary matrix A to capture the aggregate feature-latent moment, while each inner term OTiA,mΦ ,ϵ (µi , ν) is a standard EOT problem

items.text: Theorem 5: for fixed eps, the two-sample error E|S_eps({mu^i},nu) - S_eps({mu_hat^i_n}, nu_hat_n)| and the one-sample error E|S_eps({mu^i},nu) - S_eps({mu_hat^i_n}, nu)| are both O(n^{-1/2}) (constants depend on M, R, d_z, kappa, eps, sigma, with q_{R,z} = ceil((R v d_z)/2)) plus a truncation term proportional to sigma eta_R. This is the claim the synthetic experiment checks.
items.quote: the empirical full-kernel objective converges to its population counterpart up to a kernel truncation error of order ηR and a statistical error that decays at the parametric rate n−1/2

items.text: Empirical measures: mu_hat^i_n = (1/n) sum_k delta_{x^i_k} for each modality and nu_hat_n = (1/n) sum_l delta_{z_l}, with z_1..z_n drawn i.i.d. from nu independently of the modality samples.
items.quote: and let z1 , . . . , zn ∼ ν, indepen- dently of the modality samples. We define the empirical measures as

items.text: Discrete JK-EGW (Eq. 4). Each pi_hat^i is an n x n nonnegative matrix with pi_hat^i 1 = (1/n) 1 and pi_hat^{i T} 1 = (1/n) 1; pi_hat^i_{kl} is the mass from x^i_k to latent point z_l. S_hat_eps = min sum_{i,j} sum_{k,k',l,l'} W^{i,j}_{k,k'} pi^i_{k,l} pi^j_{k',l'} ||z_l - z_l'||^2 + eps sum_i KL(pi^i || mu_hat^i_n (x) nu_hat_n), with W^{i,j}_{k,k'} = K(x^i_k, x^j_k').
items.quote: These empirical transport plans are parametrized by n × n (scaled) doubly stochastic matrices,

items.text: Global block kernel matrix W in R^{N x N}, N = M n, whose (i,j) block is W^{i,j} with entries K(x^i_k, x^j_k'). Rows/columns are ordered modality by modality (modality 1 samples first).
items.quote: We further concatenate all W i,j matrices into W ∈ RN ×N , where N = M n.

items.text: Nystrom-style low-rank factor W ~= L L^T, L in R^{N x R_hat}, computed once (before Algorithm 1) by pivoted Cholesky: greedily choose pivot columns using the residual diagonal, stop when the residual trace tr(W - L L^T) falls below tolerance tau_{R_hat} > 0. The residual is PSD, so rho_{R_hat} = max_{a,b} |W_ab - (LL^T)_ab| <= tau_{R_hat}. Cost O(N R_hat) kernel evaluations, O(N R_hat^2) arithmetic, O(N R_hat) memory. References: Williams and Seeger 2000; Harbrecht et al. 2012.
items.quote: the Pivoted Cholesky factorization constructs L greedily from selected R̂ pivot columns, terminating once the residual trace tr(W − LL⊤ ) falls below a prescribed tolerance τR̂ > 0

items.text: Computable objective S_hat_eps^{R_hat} (Eq. 5): Eq. 4 with W replaced by L L^T. Matrix form (Appendix C.1): min_Pi tr(Pi^T L L^T Pi D(Z)) + eps sum_i KL(pi^i || mu_hat^i (x) nu_hat), with D(Z) = diag(ZZ^T) 1^T + 1 diag(ZZ^T)^T - 2 Z Z^T (squared-distance matrix of latent points).
items.quote: We therefore denote by ŜϵR̂ the empirical objective obtained from Equation (4) after replacing the global block matrix W by its rank-R̂ approximation LL⊤ .

items.text: Stacked plan Pi_hat = [pi_hat^1; ...; pi_hat^M] in R^{N x n}. Z_hat in R^{n x d_z} has rows z_l^T; Z_norm = (||z_1||^2, ..., ||z_n||^2)^T (squared norms). Omega = (1/n) Rowsum(L L^T) = (1/n) L (L^T 1_N) in R^N.
items.quote: We use Ẑ ∈ Rn×dz to denote the latent embedding matrix whose ℓ-th row is zℓ⊤ , and define Ẑnorm = (∥z1 ∥2 , . . . , ∥zn ∥2 )⊤ as the row-norm vector of Ẑ.

items.text: Theorem 8 (empirical lifting). S_hat_eps^{R_hat} = min over A_hat in R^{R_hat x d_z} of { 2||A_hat||_F^2 + sum_i OT^i_{C^i(A_hat),eps}(mu_hat^i_n, nu_hat_n) }, with cost C(A_hat) = 2 Omega Z_norm^T - 4 L A_hat Z_hat^T in R^{N x n}; C^i is its i-th row block (rows (i-1)n+1 .. in). Each subproblem is min_{pi^i} <C^i, pi^i> + eps KL(pi^i || mu_hat^i (x) nu_hat_n). For fixed plans, the minimising auxiliary variable is A_hat = L^T Pi_hat Z_hat.
items.quote: Moreover, for fixed transport plans {π̂ i }M i=1 , the minimizing auxiliary variable satisfies Â = L⊤ Π̂Ẑ.

items.text: Algorithm 1 (alternating minimisation for S_hat_eps^{R_hat}). Input L, Z_hat, A_hat^(0), eps, tolerance tau, T_max. (1) Z_norm <- squared row norms; (2) Omega <- (1/n) L (L^T 1_N); (3) J^(0) <- +inf. For t = 1..T_max: (5) C^(t) <- 2 Omega Z_norm^T - 4 L A_hat^(t-1) Z_hat^T; (6-9) for each modality i, pi^{i,(t)} <- Sinkhorn(C^{i,(t)}, eps; (1/n)1, (1/n)1); (10) stack into Pi^(t); (11) A_hat^(t) <- L^T Pi^(t) Z_hat; (12) J^(t) <- 2||A_hat^(t)||_F^2 + <2 Omega Z_norm^T - 4 L A_hat^(t) Z_hat^T, Pi^(t)> + eps sum_i KL(pi^{i,(t)} || mu_hat^i (x) nu_hat); (13) stop if t > 1 and |J^(t-1) - J^(t)| / (1 + |J^(t-1)|) < tau. Return (Pi^(t), A_hat^(t), J^(t)). Note: J^(t) uses the updated A_hat^(t) in the cost, not the A_hat^(t-1) used for the Sinkhorn step. Per-iteration Sinkhorn cost O(M n^2).
items.quote: Algorithm 1 Alternating minimization algorithm for solving ŜϵR̂

items.text: The per-modality EOT subproblems are solved by Sinkhorn (Cuturi 2013); the experiments use the POT library (Flamary et al. 2021), and the synthetic example uses log-domain Sinkhorn. The regulariser in the paper is eps * KL(pi || mu (x) nu); with uniform marginals this differs from POT's eps * sum pi (log pi - 1) only by a constant, so the plan is the same but objective values must include the KL form.
items.quote: Algorithm 1 implements the Sinkhorn updates (Cuturi, 2013) to solve the modality-wise EOT subproblems whose costs are determined by current auxiliary matrix Â.

items.text: Initial auxiliary matrix A_hat^(0) is an input of Algorithm 1; the paper never says how it is chosen in any experiment.
items.assumption: Use A_hat^(0) = L^T Pi_0 Z_hat with Pi_0 the independent coupling (every entry 1/n^2), which equals (1/n^2) L^T 1_N 1_n^T Z_hat. This is the closed-form update evaluated at the max-entropy plan, so the first Sinkhorn step starts from a feasible point. Since the problem is nonconvex, record the choice; if results differ, also try a few random Gaussian initialisations and keep the lowest J.

items.text: Outer stopping tolerance tau and maximum iterations T_max of Algorithm 1 are not given for any experiment.
items.assumption: tau = 1e-9 and T_max = 500 for the synthetic example (the paper treats optimisation error as negligible and Figure 4 Right reaches ~1e-13, so a tight tolerance is needed); tau = 1e-6, T_max = 200 for the larger real-data runs.

items.text: Inner Sinkhorn iteration cap and stopping threshold are not stated.
items.assumption: Log-domain Sinkhorn (POT ot.sinkhorn with method='sinkhorn_log'), stopThr = 1e-12 and numItermax = 10000 for the synthetic example; POT defaults (stopThr=1e-9, numItermax=1000) are too loose for errors near 1e-13.

items.text: Theorem 9: E|S_eps({mu^i},nu) - S_hat_eps^{R_hat}({mu_hat^i_n}, nu_hat_n)| <~ (statistical n^{-1/2} term of Theorem 5) + sigma^2 eta_R + E[rho_{R_hat}], and with rho_{R_hat} <= tau_{R_hat} a.s. the last term is tau_{R_hat}. Propositions 10-12 bound the analytic-to-computable gap by M^2 sigma (eta_R + E[rho_{R_hat}]).
items.quote: we introduce the Theorem 9 to bound the expectation between Sϵ and ŜϵR̂ .

items.text: Displayed latent point for sample x^i_k is its barycentric embedding y_hat^i_k = n sum_l pi_hat^i_{kl} z_l (Section 5.1). Section 5.3 uses Z_hat_train^txt = pi_hat^txt Z_hat and Z_hat_train^img = pi_hat^img Z_hat, the same up to the factor n.
items.quote: The displayed point for sample xik is its barycentric latent embedding

items.text: Multi-modality numerals (UCI Multiple Features, Duin 1998), digits 0-9. M = 2 modalities: 76 Fourier coefficients of character shapes (FT) and 64 Karhunen-Loeve coefficients (KL).
items.quote: The modality first consists of 76 Fourier coefficients of the character shapes

items.text: Numerals kernel: within-modality blocks W^{i,i} use RBF kernels; cross-modality blocks W^{i,j} are label agreement, W^{i,j}_{k,k'} = 1 if x^i_k and x^j_k' have the same digit label, else 0. Latent support sampled from a 2D Gaussian reference.
items.quote: we set Wk,k′ = 1 when xik and xjk′ have the same digit label and Wk,k′ = 0 otherwise.

items.text: For the numerals example the paper does not give: n (samples used), RBF bandwidth for each view, feature standardisation, the 2D Gaussian's mean/covariance, eps, R_hat or tau_{R_hat}, or the seed.
items.assumption: Use all 2000 samples (200 per digit, the full UCI set) with features z-scored per view, RBF bandwidth = median pairwise distance per view, nu = N(0, I_2), eps = 0.05 * median of the initial cost, tau_{R_hat} = 1e-6 * tr(W), seed 0. This is a qualitative figure only (Figure 2), so treat it as illustration, not a graded result.

items.text: Figure 2: 2D barycentric latent embeddings for the FT and KL views coloured by digit class; same-digit samples from both views occupy comparable regions. Qualitative only, no numbers.
items.quote: Points show the barycentric latent embeddings induced by the learned transport plans and are colored by digit class.

items.text: Synthetic example: M = 2 modalities; each marginal mu^i is supported on the same uniform grid of 20 points in [0,1] (1D), with weights from a discrete mixture of Gaussians (shown in Figure 3, peak mass ~0.11).
items.quote: The marginal distribution of each is supported on a discrete 1D set of a uniform grid of 20 points in [0, 1].

items.text: The mixture-of-Gaussian weights of mu^1 and mu^2 on the 20-point grid (component means, widths, mixing proportions) are only drawn in Figure 3, never given numerically.
items.assumption: Read approximate weights off Figure 3 if possible; otherwise use mu^1 proportional to 0.5 N(0.25, 0.08^2) + 0.5 N(0.7, 0.08^2) and mu^2 proportional to 0.4 N(0.3, 0.1^2) + 0.6 N(0.75, 0.08^2), evaluated on the grid linspace(0,1,20) and normalised. Only the slope of the error curve (about -1/2) is checked, which should not depend strongly on these weights.

items.text: Latent reference nu is uniform on a 7 x 7 grid in [-1,1]^2 (49 atoms, d_z = 2), i.e. linspace(-1,1,7) in each coordinate.
items.quote: The latent reference ν is the uniform distribution on a 7 × 7 grid in [−1, 1]2 .

items.text: Synthetic kernel: K(x,x') = gamma exp(-||x-x'||^2 / (2 l^2)) with l = 0.1, gamma = 1 within a modality and gamma = 0.6 across modalities. So over the 40 support atoms (20 per modality) the Gram matrix is [[G, 0.6 G], [0.6 G, G]] with G the 20x20 RBF Gram; PSD for gamma in [0,1], kappa = 1.
items.quote: with bandwidth ℓ = 0.1 as the similarity kernels, where γ = 1 for within-modality affinity and γ = 0.6 for cross-modality affinity.

items.text: The population value S_eps({mu^i}, nu) is computed by running Algorithm 1 on the population weights: exact Mercer features come from the eigendecomposition of the finite Gram matrix (here W itself, so L can be the full eigen-factor), and the marginals are the non-uniform mixture weights and the uniform 49-point nu.
items.quote: running Algorithm 1 on the population weights returns the ground-truth value up to solver tolerances.

items.text: Algorithm 1 and Theorem 8 are written for uniform marginals and square n x n plans. The population run (non-uniform mu^i on 20 atoms vs nu on 49 atoms) and the one-sample run (mu_hat^i_n with n atoms vs nu with 49 atoms) need weighted, rectangular versions, which the paper does not write out.
items.assumption: Generalise with weights: let a^i be the weights of modality i, b the latent weights, and D_a = diag(a^1,...,a^M). Use Omega = L (L^T a), where a stacks all a^i (this reduces to (1/n) L L^T 1_N under uniform weights), C = 2 Omega Z_norm^T - 4 L A Z^T, Sinkhorn with marginals (a^i, b), A = L^T Pi Z, and KL(pi^i || a^i b^T). Equivalently, build the empirical measures on the fixed support with counts/n as weights (repeated draws merge into one atom), so the empirical and population runs share one code path.

items.text: Parametric-rate experiment: n in {50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600}. For each n, sample mu_hat^1_n, mu_hat^2_n and nu_hat_n independently. Two-sample error |S_eps({mu_hat^i_n}, nu_hat_n) - S_eps({mu^i}, nu)|; one-sample error |S_eps({mu_hat^i_n}, nu) - S_eps({mu^i}, nu)|. Averaged over 100 Monte Carlo repetitions.
items.quote: For each n ∈ {50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1600}, we sample and construct empirical measures µ̂1n , µ̂2n , and ν̂n , independently across modalities and the latent reference

items.text: 100 Monte Carlo repetitions for both the one-sample and two-sample error curves.
items.quote: We run both experiments over 100 Monte Carlo repetitions and plot the averaged error curves on Figure 4 (Left)

items.text: The entropic parameter eps for the parametric-rate experiment (Figure 4 Left) is not stated; eps = 0.2 is given only for the truncation experiment.
items.assumption: Use eps = 0.2, the only value the paper states for this synthetic setup (Section 5.2, truncation paragraph); it is the most likely shared setting.

items.text: Random seeds for the Monte Carlo draws are not given.
items.assumption: Seed repetition r (0..99) with numpy default_rng(r) and draw modality 1, modality 2, then latent samples from that generator in that order; the curve averages over 100 draws, so the seed choice matters little.

items.text: Figure 4 Left: mean absolute error vs n (log-log) for the one-sample and two-sample regimes, both following the n^{-1/2} reference line (errors of order 1e-2). Shape only, no tabulated values. Note: the x-axis ticks read 2^6..2^10 while the stated n range is 50..1600.
items.quote: Mean absolute error of the plug-in estimator versus n (log–log), in the one-sample (ν known) and two-sample (ν estimated) regimes.

items.text: Kernel-truncation experiment kernels, common length scale l = 0.15: RBF exp(-||x-x'||^2/(2 l^2)); exponential exp(-||x-x'||/l); rational quadratic (1 + ||x-x'||^2/(2 l^2))^{-1}; periodic exp(-2 sin^2(pi ||x-x'||)/l^2).
items.quote: We set a common length scale ℓ = 0.15 to all the kernels that approximately matches the geometry in the feature space.

items.text: Entropic regularisation eps = 0.2 for the kernel-truncation experiment.
items.quote: We still use Algorithm 1 to solve for the transport plan with the entropy regularization parameter ϵ = 0.2.

items.text: Rank-R features Phi_R come from the top R eigenpairs of the kernel Gram matrix on the finite support (40 atoms for 2 modalities x 20 grid points); S_eps uses the full eigensystem. Report |S_eps - S_eps^R| against R (Figure 4 Right shows R from 0 to ~50).
items.quote: the rank-R features ΦR are formed by by retaining the top R leading eigenpairs of the kernel Gram matrix.

items.text: For the four truncation kernels the paper does not say whether the cross-modality scaling gamma = 0.6 is still applied, or whether the Gram matrix is eigendecomposed with or without the rho weights (Mercer w.r.t. rho vs plain Gram matrix).
items.assumption: Keep gamma = 1 within / 0.6 across, as in the rest of Section 5.2, and eigendecompose the plain 40x40 Gram matrix (the text says 'kernel Gram matrix'). Truncation in Algorithm 1 then means L = U_R diag(sqrt(lambda_R)). Sweep R from 1 to 50 (the Gram has rank <= 40, so the gap reaches solver precision at R <= 40).

items.text: Figure 4 Right: |S_eps - S_eps^R| decreases with R for all four kernels (log scale from ~1e-1 down to ~1e-13); RBF and rational quadratic reach solver precision faster, exponential and periodic need larger R. Shape only, no tabulated values.
items.quote: Among the 4 kernels, the smooth RBF and rational quadratic kernels reach solver precision faster, whereas the exponential and periodic kernels require larger R.

items.text: MS-COCO 2017 train split; each image paired with the concatenation of its five captions. Class-targeted balanced sampling, each image assigned to at most one target category, disjoint train/test. 6K subset: 20 categories, 300 train + 150 test per category (6000 train, 3000 test). 9K subset: 30 categories, 300 train + 100 test per category (9000 train, 3000 test).
items.quote: a 6K subset with 6000 training and 3000 test images drawn from 20 categories (300 training and 150 test images per category)

items.text: Which MS-COCO categories are selected, and how 'assigned to at most one target category' is decided for multi-label images, is not given.
items.assumption: Take the 20 (6K) / 30 (9K) categories with the most images in train2017, and keep only images whose annotations contain exactly one of the selected categories; sample 300 + 150 (or 100) per category with a fixed seed. This is a guess, so retrieval numbers will only be roughly comparable.

items.text: Frozen encoders: MPNet (Song et al. 2020) for text, DINOv3 (Simeoni et al. 2025) for images. Features extracted once and l2-normalised before alignment and evaluation.
items.quote: We use MPNet (Song et al., 2020) as the frozen text encoder and DI- NOv3 (Siméoni et al., 2025) as the frozen image encoder.

items.text: Exact checkpoints (MPNet variant, DINOv3 size/patch, pooling, which layer) are not named.
items.assumption: sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2 (mean pooling) for captions and facebook/dinov3-vitb16 CLS token for images; these are the common public defaults for these encoder families.

items.text: Latent reference nu: Gaussian mixture with 20 isotropic components whose means lie along mutually orthogonal directions at a fixed distance from the origin; latent dimension d = 32 (Table 1). Ablation d in {32, 48, 64, 128}.
items.quote: The distribution ν is instantiates as a Gaussian mixture model with 20 components. Each component follows an isotropic Gaussian, whose means are placed along mutually orthogonal directions

items.text: GMM mean distance from origin, component variance, mixing weights, the number of latent support points n, and whether the 9K run (30 categories) still uses 20 components are not given.
items.assumption: Means = r * e_c for the first 20 standard basis vectors (r = 1), component std 0.1, equal weights, 20 components for both subsets as stated; n latent points = number of training pairs used in Algorithm 1 (6000 or 9000, minus validation), as Section 4 requires n latent points for n samples.

items.text: Section 5.3 never says how the global kernel W is built for MS-COCO (within-modality similarity, cross-modality affinity from pairs and/or category labels, bandwidths), nor eps, R_hat or tau_{R_hat}.
items.assumption: Follow Section 5.1 / the introduction: within-modality blocks = RBF on l2-normalised features with bandwidth = median pairwise distance; cross-modality block = 1 for the true image-caption pair and for same-category pairs, 0 otherwise. eps = 0.01 times the mean of the initial cost; pivoted Cholesky tolerance tau_{R_hat} = 1e-4 * tr(W). Mark any MS-COCO reproduction as approximate because of this gap.

items.text: Out-of-sample map: per modality, train an MLP that regresses raw (l2-normalised) encoder features X_train onto the l2-normalised training embeddings Z_hat_train = pi_hat Z_hat. Model selection on a small validation split held out from training, by validation R@1. MLPs are frozen and applied to l2-normalised test features.
items.quote: we train a simple MLP for each modality that regresses the raw encoder features Xtrain onto the (ℓ2 -normalized) training Ẑtrain .

items.text: MLP architecture, loss, optimiser, epochs, learning rate and validation split size are not given.
items.assumption: 2-layer MLP (hidden 1024, GELU), MSE loss, Adam lr 1e-3, up to 200 epochs with early stopping on validation R@1, 10% of training pairs held out for validation.

items.text: Baselines: CSA (Li et al. 2025), closed-form canonical similarity analysis via CCA; CSA+STRUCTURE (CSA with the similarity-based layer selection and STRUCTURE regulariser of Groger et al. 2025); MLP+STRUCTURE (trainable MLP head with contrastive objective, layer selection and STRUCTURE regularisation). Hyperparameters are not given; use the cited papers' defaults.
items.quote: CSA (Li et al., 2025) is a closed- form canonical similarity analysis method that maps frozen unimodal features into a shared multimodal space

items.text: Alignment metrics on the pooled test image and caption embeddings with target-category labels: purity of a k-means clustering of the pooled embeddings vs categories; silhouette score with cosine distance using category labels.
items.quote: Purity measures the agreement between a k-means clustering of the pooled embeddings and the target categories

items.text: The k-means k, initialisation and seed used for purity are not stated.
items.assumption: k = number of categories (20 or 30), scikit-learn KMeans with n_init=10, random_state=0, on the pooled 6000 test embeddings (3000 images + 3000 captions).

items.text: Retrieval by cosine similarity between aligned test embeddings. R@k img->txt = (1/n_ev) sum_i 1{r_i^{img->txt} <= k}, where r_i is the rank of image i's paired caption among all test captions; txt->img defined symmetrically; reported R@k = (R@k img->txt + R@k txt->img)/2, k in {1, 5}.
items.quote: the image-to-text recall is

items.text: Table 1-3 numbers are single values with no error bars; the number of runs and seeds (subset sampling, latent sampling, MLP training) are not given.
items.assumption: Treat each table cell as one run with seed 0 and report run-to-run spread over at least 3 seeds alongside, since a single-seed comparison at tolerance 0.01 is not meaningful given the unspecified kernel, encoders and categories.
